strengths: The paper gives a clear theoretical treatment of multi-modal variational distribution matching: Proposition 1 and Corollary 2 characterize how the proposed marginal plus conditional objective relates to KL divergences and when it approximates the multi-modal log-likelihood.

It provides an information-theoretic rate-distortion perspective (Lemma 7 and Corollary 8), making precise how the proposed objective differs from mixture-based bounds and why mixture-based bounds can have an irreducible gap even with flexible encoders.

The proposed permutation-invariant aggregation schemes (DeepSets/SumPooling and Set Transformer/SelfAttention variants, plus equivariant private-latent extensions) are natural, flexible generalizations of PoE/MoE and can condition on arbitrary modality subsets without explicitly enumerating all subsets.

The empirical study is broad, spanning linear Gaussian models, nonlinear identifiable synthetic models, and MNIST-SVHN-Text, with evaluations of log-likelihood, MCC, generative coherence, and rate-distortion trade-offs.
The paper is reasonably reproducible: it includes detailed pseudo-code, architectural tables, hyperparameters, missing-modality protocols, and compute-resource information in the appendices.
The limitations section is honest about increased computational cost and about cases where mixture-based bounds may be preferable, especially for cross-modal reconstruction.
The work connects multi-modal VAEs to neural processes/meta-learning and to identifiability, which gives useful conceptual context beyond a purely empirical contribution.
weaknesses: The central objective is only an approximate lower bound on the multi-modal log-likelihood. The term E_q[log q(z|x_S)/p(z|x_S)] can be positive, so with finite-capacity encoders the bound may not be valid and optimizing L_S and L_{\S} may pull q(z|x_S) in conflicting directions. The claim of a 'tighter variational bound' is therefore not guaranteed in the practical regime.

The permutation-invariant aggregation contribution is mostly the application of standard DeepSets/Set Transformer architectures to multi-modal VAE aggregation. The novelty is moderate, and it is not fully isolated from other choices such as additional capacity or hyperparameter tuning in PoE+/MoE+ baselines.

The identifiability discussion relies on strong assumptions: exponential-family posterior, injective decoders, Lebesgue densities, exact posterior approximation, and no discrete modalities. The empirical MCC gains are often small or inconsistent, so the link between flexible aggregation and improved identifiability is suggestive rather than firmly established.

The main MNIST-SVHN-Text log-likelihood comparison is against the authors' own mixture-based bound rather than strong external multi-modal VAE baselines under matched settings. The external baselines are reported only for coherence/classification and differ in decoder-variance assumptions, weakening the comparative evidence.

The results show substantial trade-offs: the proposed bound often improves joint log-likelihood but can worsen cross-modal coherence and unsupervised latent classification compared with mixture-based bounds. Some private-latent results, e.g. SelfAttention on MNIST-SVHN-Text, favor the mixture bound.

The linear Gaussian experiments contain very large numerical values (e.g. 10^35) and unexplained relative gaps in Table 1, which raise concerns about numerical conditioning and make the practical significance of those comparisons unclear.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy, with several typos, formatting issues, missing table entries, and reference errors (e.g. using Kingma and Ba for VAE/Adam ambiguously). This makes some results harder to verify than necessary.

The method is computationally more expensive because it requires sampling from two encoding distributions and learning aggregation networks, but no runtime, memory, or scaling comparisons are provided. Scalability to larger numbers of modalities is not empirically demonstrated.

strengths: Proposes a principled multimodal variational bound that combines marginal and conditional ELBO terms with arbitrary modality masking, generalizing Wu and Goodman (2019) to M modalities and providing ELBO surgery (Proposition 1) and a log-likelihood approximation (Corollary 2) with explicit tightness conditions.

Introduces flexible permutation-invariant and permutation-equivariant aggregation schemes based on DeepSets/Set Transformers for multimodal encoders, enabling conditioning on arbitrary modality subsets and handling private latent variables in a unified way.

Provides extensive experiments across linear Gaussian models, nonlinear identifiable models, and MNIST-SVHN-Text, comparing multiple aggregation schemes and bounds with rate-distortion, reconstruction, coherence, and identifiability metrics.
Includes an honest limitations discussion and useful connections to neural processes, MoPoE, VampPriors, and information-theoretic rate-distortion trade-offs.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the proposed objective is essentially a combination of standard marginal and conditional ELBOs and is closely related to neural process objectives and existing multimodal bounds; the permutation-invariant aggregation is a natural application of existing set networks, and the paper does not prove that its family includes PoE or MoE as special cases.

The central claim of a 'tighter variational bound' is not rigorously established. The proposed objective is not a true lower bound because the gap to the log-likelihood contains a term that can be positive (Corollary 2 and Remark 3). The paper does not directly measure bound tightness (bound value versus log-likelihood) but instead compares downstream test LLH of learned models.

Evaluation lacks apples-to-apples comparisons with established multimodal VAE baselines such as MoPoE, MMVAE+, and MVTCAE under identical architectures and hyperparameters. External baseline numbers are not directly comparable due to different decoder variances and training setups. No code release is mentioned, and the pseudo-code appears to contain typos (e.g., Algorithm 1 samples z_S from x_M).

The identifiability contribution is largely adapted from Lu et al. (2022), and the empirical MCC gains are marginal or absent in several settings (e.g., SumPooling invariantly gives MCC 0.84 for both bounds; mixture-based bounds match or exceed the proposed bound in some cases), so the claim that the new bound specifically aids identifiability is weakly supported.

Practical benefits are mixed: the method improves full log-likelihood but often worsens cross-modal reconstruction and some coherence/classification metrics. The experiments are limited to synthetic data and MNIST-SVHN-Text despite motivation from multi-omics and neuroscience applications.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy, with typographical and numbering inconsistencies (e.g., Corollary 2 versus Corollary 19, 'L_{\backslash \mathcal{L}}' typos, grammatical errors), which hinders readability and reproducibility.

strengths: The paper proposes a general multi-modal variational bound that can condition on arbitrary modality subsets, together with a clear distribution-matching and information-theoretic analysis (Proposition 1, Lemma 7, Corollary 8). This provides a useful unifying view of several conditional VAE, neural-process, and multimodal VAE objectives.

It introduces permutation-invariant and permutation-equivariant aggregation schemes based on DeepSets/Set Transformer modules, which are well motivated for encoding modality subsets and for private latent variables. The appendices provide algorithms, architectures, and implementation details, supporting reproducibility.

The empirical study is broad and consistent: synthetic linear models, nonlinear identifiable models, and MNIST-SVHN-Text experiments generally show that the proposed bound and the flexible aggregation schemes improve log-likelihood, reconstruction, and in some cases MCC/identifiability.

The manuscript is mostly well structured and includes an honest limitations discussion, including the extra computational cost of sampling from two encoding distributions and the potential preference for mixture-based bounds when cross-modal reconstruction is the primary goal.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited. The proposed bound is closely related to existing conditional VAE / neural-process objectives and to Wu and Goodman's multi-modal bound; Proposition 1 and Corollary 2 are essentially standard ELBO surgery, and the identifiability result is an adaptation of an existing theorem from Lu et al. (2022). The permutation-invariant encoders are a natural but largely direct application of known DeepSets and Set Transformer architectures to multimodal VAEs.

The central claim of a 'tighter variational bound' is qualified: the objective is not a true lower bound in general because of the extra term in Corollary 19. The paper shows tightness only in an infinite-capacity limit, and does not provide finite-sample or practical conditions under which the approximation gap is controlled. This weakens the strength of the claimed advantage over mixture-based bounds.

The empirical comparisons with prior work are not fully convincing. The reported log-likelihood values, especially in Table 5, are not directly comparable to earlier multimodal VAE results because of different decoder variance choices, likelihood weighting, and evaluation protocols. Some external baselines appear only in selected tables with many NA entries, so the claimed superiority over existing methods is not cleanly established.

The identifiability section is somewhat disconnected from the proposed method. Proposition 15 assumes that the variational posterior exactly matches the true posterior and that the model is strongly exponential; it does not show that the proposed bound or aggregation schemes improve identifiability in practice. The assumptions are strong and their violation under realistic misspecification is not analyzed.

The paper provides little analysis of computational scalability and optimization trade-offs. Self-attention scales quadratically in the number of modalities, the new bound requires two encoding distributions per gradient step, and there is no wall-clock or memory comparison against PoE/MoE/MoPoE-style baselines. This limits practical guidance for large M.

There are presentation and notation issues, including inconsistent numbering (e.g., 'Corollary 19', 'Remark 3' references), a typo such as \mathcal{L}_{\backslash\mathcal{L}}, and occasional unclear figure/table descriptions. These are not fatal but reduce polish and reliability of the exposition.
